title: The timeless Test of 1939
hook: A cricket match meant to last until someone won was stopped so England could catch a ship.
peek: In 1939 England and South Africa played a Test match in Durban with no time limit. After 12 days it had to be called off as a draw, because the England team had a boat home to catch.
lede: Some Test matches in the 1930s were timeless: they would be played to a finish, however long it took. The fifth Test between South Africa and England at Durban began on 3 March 1939. On 14 March, with England chasing a huge target and needing just 42 more runs, it was abandoned as a draw. The team had to leave for their ship home.

bullets.text: England were set 696 to win in the fourth innings and reached 654 for 5. The match produced 1,981 runs, still the most in any Test.
Bill Edrich had struggled all series, yet he made 219 in England's second innings, the score that made the chase look possible.
England had to take a train to Cape Town to board the Athlone Castle for the voyage home. Rain on the final day ended any hope of finishing first.
The match helped end the idea. No Test since has been played without a time limit, and today's Tests last at most five days.
